extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, appellate judges, and patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether claims in a reissue patent comply with the original-patent requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 251 (and related rule against recapture), including what must be disclosed in the original specification and what evidence is legally sufficient. Applied in appellate review of district-court determinations of reissue validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original-patent requirement (35 U.S.C. § 251)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may grant a reissue patent “for the invention disclosed in the original patent.” Reissue claims must satisfy the original-patent requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require that the invention claimed on reissue be more than merely suggested or indicated by the original specification; the specification of the original patent "must clearly and unequivocally disclose the newly claimed invention as a separate invention." (Antares, Forum). The reissue claim must be for the "exact embodiment claimed on reissue [that is] expressly disclosed in the specification." If the exact embodiment is missing from the original specification, the reissue claim is invalid under § 251.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express-disclosure vs. inference standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the original-patent requirement, disclosure must appear on the face of the original patent; inferences that a person of ordinary skill would draw are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony about what a skilled artisan would understand from the specification (i.e., that the specification 'encompasses' the claimed subject matter) cannot substitute for an express disclosure. The focus is on what is apparent "from the face of the instrument," not on post-hoc expert inferences. Relying on broad embodiments to show express disclosure of a narrower, unexpressed embodiment is too lenient under precedent (Industrial Chemicals, Forum, Antares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corbin/Industrial Chemicals "more than merely suggested" principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue claims cannot be based on subject matter that is merely suggested or indicated in the original patent; it must appear that the subject matter was intended to be covered by the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Corbin and Industrial Chemicals: new and broader claims must not be merely suggested; they must constitute parts or portions of the invention intended or sought to be covered by the original patent. Courts applying § 251 continue to apply this principle when assessing whether the reissue covers the same invention disclosed originally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule against recapture
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue cannot reclaim subject matter surrendered during prosecution of the original patent (i.e., reclaimed subject matter surrendered during prosecution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reissue validity, courts examine whether the reissue claims attempt to recapture subject matter disclaimed or surrendered earlier; such recapture is barred. (Mentioned as a discrete legal issue to be evaluated alongside the original-patent requirement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity of reissue claims (under § 251) must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court concluded Google had not proven invalidity under § 251 by clear and convincing evidence; appellate review considers whether that burden was met under applicable precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standard and appellate review (who decides / standard of review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with § 251 is a question of law reviewed de novo, although it can involve underlying questions of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the legal conclusion can involve factual determinations, courts may consider expert evidence to understand technical terms. Still, the ultimate determination whether the original patent unmistakably discloses the reissue invention is a legal one for the court (appellate courts review de novo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible role of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert evidence may be used to ascertain the meaning of technical or scientific terms, but experts cannot supply an express disclosure that is absent from the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts can aid the court in understanding what the instruments say (technical meaning of terms), but testimony that a skilled artisan would infer or understand an embodiment from the specification is insufficient to meet the express-disclosure requirement. Forum explained that testimony about what a skilled artisan would infer is inadequate to satisfy Industrial Chemicals/Antares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact-embodiment requirement (expressness and specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must expressly disclose the exact embodiment claimed on reissue; a general or broader disclosure that merely "encompasses" the narrower claimed embodiment is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court explained that a skilled artisan might well infer the claimed embodiment from a broader disclosure (and expert testimony supported that), but precedent requires an express disclosure of the exact embodiment. The opinion emphasizes that expressness means the embodiment containing the precise claimed features (e.g., two web browser processes) appears in the original specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative inference gaps (application example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When mapping a claimed reissue embodiment to an original specification, multiple specific inferences may be required; if those inferences are necessary rather than the embodiment being expressly described, § 251 is not satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an example, the court identified three inferences a skilled artisan would need to draw from the original specification to arrive at the reissue claims in this case: (1) that an "interactive network process" includes web browsing, (2) that "interactive network process status data" includes website data, and (3) that a web browser process could be executed on the processor identified (P1). Requiring such inferential leaps shows the absence of an express disclosure and thus failure to meet § 251.
